title: Permutation and Its Conditions
description: This lesson introduces permutations as ordered arrangements, explains why order matters, and explores how specific conditions like fixed positions or grouping affect permutations.

sections:
What is a Permutation? 
A permutation is an ordered arrangement of objects. Changing the order creates a new arrangement.

Example 1: 
List all the possible three-letter arrangement in the word EAR. 
\quad E -> A -> R  ---- E A R 
\quad E -> R -> A  ---- E R A 
\quad A -> E -> R  ---- A E R 
\quad A -> R -> E  ---- A R E 
\quad R -> E -> A  ---- R E A 
\quad R -> A -> E  ---- R A E

Example 2: 
How many three-letter arrangements in the word EAR can be formed satisfying the given conditions. 
\quad A. the first letter is E 
\quad B. the vowels are together 
\quad C. the vowels must NOT be together 
Solutions 
\small \quad A. There are 2 arrangements formed whose first letter is E. Those are EAR and E 
\small \quad B. There are 4 arrangements formed wherein the vowels are together. Those are E 
\small \quad C. There are 2 arrangements formed wherein the vowels are NOT together. Those are ERA and ARE.

Why Order Matters 
In permutations, the order of arrangement is important. ABC and BAC are considered different arrangements.

Types of Conditions 
\small \quad Case 1: An element must be in a specific position (e.g., Bobby must be first). 
\small \quad Case 2: Two or more elements must be together (e.g., friends sit side by side). 
\small \quad Case 3: Two or more elements must not be together (e.g., books not next to each other).

Summary 
A permutation is an arrangement where order matters. Conditions can limit or define how objects are arranged.
